data.name: Prefetch
data.takeaway: Strong execution indicator with run counts and timestamps.
data.what: Windows Prefetch (.pf) files are created when an executable runs and store run counts, last run timestamps, and referenced file paths.
data.why: Helps confirm execution and frequency; use it to anchor timelines with other artifacts.
data.question: Did this program execute on this system, and when?
corroborate: AppCompatCache or Amcache for file presence
location: Win10/11 may limit Prefetch on SSDs or when SysMain is off; absence is not proof.

data.name: LNK Files
data.takeaway: Proves a user opened a file path and captures volume context.
data.what: Windows shortcut files created when a user opens a file or folder; store target path, timestamps, volume serials, and network share metadata.
data.why: Proves user interaction even if the file moved or was deleted, and adds volume context for removable media.
data.question: Was this file opened or accessed by a user?
corroborate: Browser history if the file came from a download

data.name: RecentDocs
data.takeaway: Fast view of recently opened file names grouped by extension.
data.what: Per-user registry lists of recently opened files grouped by extension, storing MRU order and entry names.
data.why: Quickly surfaces filenames and usage order when higher-fidelity artifacts are missing.
data.question: What files did the user open recently?

data.name: UserAssist
data.takeaway: Shows GUI-launched programs per user with last run time.
data.what: Per-user registry data tracking GUI launches (ROT13 encoded values) with run counts and timestamps.
data.why: Shows user-driven execution and rough timing for GUI-launched programs.
data.question: What programs did the user launch from the GUI?

data.name: AppCompatCache (Shimcache)
data.takeaway: Useful for file presence; execution inference varies by OS.
data.what: Legacy compatibility cache entries populated by AppCompat routines, recording file paths and metadata rather than guaranteed execution.
data.why: Useful evidence of file presence or compatibility checks; treat timestamps cautiously and corroborate.
data.question: Was this binary or path present on the system?
location: Parsing varies by Windows version; treat as legacy evidence.

data.name: Amcache
data.takeaway: Reliable record of program presence and install metadata.
data.what: Registry hive tracking installed applications and executed binaries with file paths, hashes, publisher info, and timestamps.
data.why: Strong program presence evidence that often persists after deletion or uninstall.
data.question: Was this program installed or executed on the host?

data.name: Run Keys
data.takeaway: Common persistence path; entries should map to known binaries.
data.what: Registry keys that auto-start programs at logon for machine or user contexts, mapping value names to commands.
data.why: Highlights persistence and auto-start command lines that need validation.
data.question: What starts automatically at logon, and is it legitimate?

data.name: Scheduled Tasks
data.takeaway: Triggers and actions reveal automated execution paths.
data.what: Task definitions that run on schedule or triggers, stored as XML with actions, triggers, and principal context.
data.why: Reveals automated execution paths and the account/context used to run them.
data.question: Is anything running on a schedule that should not?
corroborate: Run keys and Startup folder items

data.name: Event Logs
data.takeaway: Authoritative event timeline for authentication, process execution, service changes, and security events.
data.what: Structured Windows event records stored in EVTX format across multiple log channels. The three primary logs (Security, System, Application) are supplemented by hundreds of operational logs for specific features and services.
data.why: Authoritative timeline for authentication, process, and service activity. Many attack techniques leave traces only in event logs. Critical for establishing user activity, lateral movement, and persistence.
data.question: When did the user log in, what processes ran, and what changed on the system?

Process Execution.timestamps: Requires audit policy; shows command line if enabled
Full command line, hashes, parent process

keyFields: Security 4624: LogonType, TargetUserName, IpAddress, WorkstationName
Security 4688: NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName (if enabled)
System 7045: ServiceName, ImagePath, ServiceType, StartType
Use wevtutil or Get-WinEvent for extraction
EvtxECmd for timeline-friendly parsing

data.name: Timeline (Plaso/Log2Timeline)
data.takeaway: Best pivot to see multi-source activity around a time window.
data.what: Aggregated timeline produced by tools like Plaso, combining file system, registry, event logs, and browser data into one sequence.
data.why: Fastest way to pivot around incident windows and spot gaps or inconsistencies across sources.
data.question: What happened before, during, and after the incident?
location: Plaso storage file (.plaso) and CSV/JSON exports
Timeline output from the Artifact Timeline workflow

data.name: Windows Defender
data.takeaway: Confirms detections and remediation actions.
data.what: Detection history, scan metadata, and quarantine records with threat names, paths, and remediation status.
data.why: Confirms security detections and the exact files or paths affected, with timestamps.
data.question: Did Defender detect or quarantine relevant files?
corroborate: File system artifacts or malware samples

data.name: Browser Artifacts
data.takeaway: Shows user intent, downloads, searches, and browsing context across all platforms.
data.what: Per-profile SQLite databases tracking URLs, downloads, searches, cookies, cached credentials, and visit timestamps. Each browser stores data differently but all provide rich forensic evidence.
data.why: Reveals user intent, initial access vectors, download sources, and browsing patterns tied to suspected activity. Critical for phishing investigations and tracking lateral movement via web interfaces.
data.question: What did the user search for, download, or visit?
corroborate: Zone.Identifier / Quarantine events for download sources

firefox.timestamps: visit_date, last_visit_date (PRTime: microseconds since Unix epoch)

edge.tables: urls, visits, downloads (Chromium-based, same as Chrome)

urls.title / moz_places.title - Page title
urls.visit_count / moz_places.visit_count - Number of visits
downloads.target_path - Where file was saved
downloads.tab_url / referrer - Source page for download
keyword_search_terms.term - Search queries
cookies.host_key - Domain for session analysis

data.name: $MFT + USN Journal
data.takeaway: Reconstructs file lifecycle even after deletion.
data.what: NTFS metadata ($MFT) storing file records and timestamps; the USN Journal records change events and reasons.
data.why: Reliable evidence of file creation, movement, and deletion even when content is gone.
data.question: What changed on disk, and when?
corroborate: Timeline entries for file creation or deletes
Relevant LNK files for user access

data.name: Recycle Bin
data.takeaway: Captures deleted file names, original paths, and deletion times.
data.what: Metadata ($I) and content ($R) for deleted items per SID, including original path and deletion time.
data.why: Shows user-initiated deletion and original location for timeline reconstruction.
data.question: What was deleted, and when?

data.name: Jump Lists
data.takeaway: App-focused record of recent files and tasks.
data.what: Per-user, per-app automatic/custom destination files capturing recent files and tasks with timestamps and paths.
data.why: Highlights app-specific user activity and the files opened through that app.
data.question: Which files or folders were opened through a specific app?

data.name: Shellbags
data.takeaway: Evidence of folder browsing, even for deleted or remote folders.
data.what: Per-user registry artifacts recording folder view settings and navigation, including folder paths and sometimes timestamps.
data.why: Evidence of folder access, including deleted or removable locations, even without file artifacts.
data.question: Which folders did the user browse?

data.name: SRUM
data.takeaway: Timeline of app and network usage per user.
data.what: SRUM database tracking app usage, network activity, and resource consumption per user over time.
data.why: Builds time-based evidence tying users to apps and network usage.
data.question: Which apps used the network or ran during the timeframe?
corroborate: Event Logs for network or logon activity

data.name: USB Device History
data.takeaway: Identifies removable devices with first/last connection times and user attribution.
data.what: Multiple registry keys and log files recording USB device installs, vendor/product IDs, serial numbers, volume serial numbers, drive letters, and connection timestamps. Cross-referencing these sources enables full device timeline reconstruction.
data.why: Critical for data exfiltration investigations. Correlating device serial numbers with user SIDs proves which user connected which device and when.
data.question: Which USB storage devices were connected, when, and by whom?
corroborate: Shellbags for volume/folder browsing on the device
$MFT/USN for file operations on removable drives
LNK files pointing to removable drive paths

data.name: Services
data.takeaway: Persistent system startup artifacts with binary paths.
data.what: Service and driver configuration stored in the registry, including start type, image path, and account context.
data.why: Surfaces persistent services and launch context for suspicious binaries.
data.question: What services or drivers are configured to start automatically?

data.name: WMI Subscriptions
data.takeaway: Stealthy persistence via filters/consumers/bindings.
data.what: WMI event filters, consumers, and bindings that can execute scripts or commands on triggers.
data.why: Stealthy persistence that bypasses common startup lists; bindings show trigger/action pairs.
data.question: Is WMI being used for persistence or tasking?

data.name: PowerShell Logs
data.takeaway: Script block and transcription logs reveal executed commands.
data.what: Event logs capturing PowerShell script execution including Script Block Logging (Event ID 4104), Module Logging, and optional transcription files.
data.why: Critical for reconstructing attacker commands, decoded payloads, and obfuscated script content.
data.question: What PowerShell commands or scripts were executed?

data.name: BITS Jobs
data.takeaway: Background transfers used for downloads and persistence.
data.what: Background Intelligent Transfer Service jobs that download or upload files asynchronously, surviving reboots and network interruptions.
data.why: Attackers abuse BITS for stealthy downloads and persistence; jobs persist across reboots.
data.question: Were BITS jobs used to download payloads or maintain persistence?

data.name: RDP Artifacts
data.takeaway: Tracks remote desktop connections both inbound (to this system) and outbound (from this system).
data.what: Registry keys storing outbound connection history, event logs recording both inbound and outbound sessions with usernames, source IPs, and timestamps. Bitmap cache files may contain screenshots of remote sessions.
data.why: Essential for tracking lateral movement. Inbound connections show who accessed this system; outbound connections show what systems this user accessed. Bitmap cache can reveal what the attacker saw.
data.question: Who connected via RDP, from where, to where, and when?
location: NTUSER.DAT\Software\Microsoft\Terminal Server Client\Servers - Outbound: servers this user connected TO
NTUSER.DAT\Software\Microsoft\Terminal Server Client\Default - Outbound: MRU of recent connections
keyFields: Terminal Server Client\Servers\<hostname> - UsernameHint shows username used
Logon Type 10 (RemoteInteractive) in Event 4624 confirms RDP
Source Network Address in Event 4624/21 shows originating IP
Bitmap cache: use bmc-tools to extract cached screen tiles

data.name: BAM/DAM
data.takeaway: Records program execution with timestamps per user.
data.what: Background Activity Moderator (BAM) and Desktop Activity Moderator (DAM) registry keys tracking executed programs with last execution timestamps.
data.why: Provides execution evidence with user context and timestamps, useful when Prefetch is disabled.
data.question: What programs did users execute recently?

data.name: TypedPaths / TypedURLs
data.takeaway: Records paths and URLs typed by the user.
data.what: Per-user registry keys storing Explorer address bar paths (TypedPaths) and Internet Explorer URLs (TypedURLs) entered manually.
data.why: Shows intentional user navigation to specific paths or sites, indicating knowledge and intent.
data.question: What paths or URLs did the user manually navigate to?

data.name: Startup Folder
data.takeaway: Simple persistence via shortcuts in startup directories.
data.what: Per-user and system-wide folders containing shortcuts or executables that run at logon.
data.why: Common and simple persistence mechanism; contents should match known legitimate software.
data.question: What programs start automatically via startup folders?
corroborate: LNK file analysis for target paths

data.name: Volume Shadow Copies
data.takeaway: Point-in-time snapshots for recovering deleted or modified files.
data.what: System restore points and shadow copies containing previous versions of files, registry hives, and system state.
data.why: Enables recovery of deleted files and comparison of system state before/after an incident.
data.question: What did the system look like before the incident?
corroborate: Current artifacts compared to shadow copy versions
location: System Volume Information on each NTFS volume
Access via mklink or forensic mounting

data.name: Alternate Data Streams
data.takeaway: Hidden data attached to files, including Zone.Identifier for downloads.
data.what: NTFS feature allowing multiple data streams per file; commonly used for Zone.Identifier (Mark of the Web) and sometimes for hiding data.
data.why: Zone.Identifier proves a file was downloaded from the internet; malicious ADS can hide payloads.
data.question: Where did this file come from, and is data hidden in alternate streams?
location: Zone.Identifier contains ZoneId and often ReferrerUrl

data.name: Windows Search Index
data.takeaway: Indexed file content and metadata, including deleted files.
data.what: Windows Search database (Windows.edb) containing indexed content, file paths, and metadata for files that may no longer exist.
data.why: Can reveal file content and existence even after deletion; useful for keyword searches.
data.question: What files existed or contained specific content?
location: Use ESEDatabaseView or dedicated forensic tools to parse

data.name: Thumbnail Cache
data.takeaway: Image previews persist even after original files are deleted.
data.what: Cached thumbnail images generated when viewing folders in Explorer, stored in thumbcache_*.db files.
data.why: Proves images existed on the system even if deleted; can recover preview versions of deleted pictures.
data.question: What images were viewed or existed on this system?
location: Use Thumbcache Viewer or similar tools

data.name: Network Shares / Mapped Drives
data.takeaway: Evidence of network resource access and lateral movement.
data.what: Registry keys and MRU lists tracking mapped network drives, recent network paths, and share connections.
data.why: Shows network resources accessed, supporting lateral movement or data access analysis.
data.question: What network shares or remote systems did the user access?
corroborate: LNK files pointing to network locations

data.name: Windows Error Reporting
data.takeaway: Crash reports can reveal exploitation or malware behavior.
data.what: Crash dump files and reports generated when applications crash, containing process state and exception information.
data.why: Exploitation attempts often cause crashes; reports may capture malicious process state.
data.question: Did any applications crash suspiciously, and what was their state?

data.name: MUICache
data.takeaway: Records executable display names, proving program presence.
data.what: Registry cache of executable display names populated when programs run, mapping paths to friendly names.
data.why: Evidence of program execution; persists even after the executable is deleted.
data.question: What programs were executed on this system?

data.name: WordWheelQuery
data.takeaway: Records searches performed in Explorer.
data.what: Per-user registry key storing recent search terms entered in Windows Explorer search boxes.
data.why: Reveals what the user was looking for; can indicate intent or awareness of specific files.
data.question: What did the user search for in Explorer?

data.name: LastVisitedMRU
data.takeaway: Tracks applications and folders used in Open/Save dialogs.
data.what: Registry keys recording which applications were used to open files and which folders were accessed via Open/Save dialogs.
data.why: Shows application-to-file relationships and folder access patterns.
data.question: Which applications opened or saved files, and where?

data.name: Network Profiles
data.takeaway: History of wired and wireless networks with first/last connection timestamps for location analysis.
data.what: Registry records of every network the system has connected to, including network names (SSIDs), network types (public/private/domain), MAC addresses of gateways, and precise first/last connection timestamps. Each network gets a unique Profile GUID.
data.why: Shows where the system has been physically located based on network connections. First connection time proves when a system first appeared on a network; last connection time shows most recent presence. Gateway MAC addresses can identify specific network infrastructure.
data.question: What networks has this system connected to, and when?
corroborate: WLAN AutoConfig logs for WiFi details
location: SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\NetworkList\Nla\Cache - Network location awareness cache
keyFields: ProfileName - Human-readable network name (SSID for WiFi)
Description - Network description
DateCreated (REG_BINARY) - First connection timestamp (SYSTEMTIME format)
DateLastConnected (REG_BINARY) - Last connection timestamp (SYSTEMTIME format)
Category - Network type: 0=Public, 1=Private, 2=Domain
NameType - 6=Wired, 23=VPN, 71=Wireless
Signatures\*\DefaultGatewayMac - Gateway MAC address (network fingerprint)
Signatures\*\DnsSuffix - DNS suffix for the network

data.name: Bash History
data.takeaway: Direct record of user commands (if not cleared).
data.what: Per-user bash command history written to HISTFILE on shell exit or periodically depending on settings.
data.why: Direct view of commands and intent; can reveal tools used and paths touched.
data.question: What commands did the user run?
location: History can be cleared or disabled.

data.name: Auth Logs
data.takeaway: Logons, sudo use, and failures by source.
data.what: Authentication and sudo logs for SSH and local logins, including source IPs and failure reasons.
data.why: Confirms access paths and privilege escalation; useful for detecting brute-force or abuse.
data.question: Who authenticated, from where, and when?

data.name: Syslog
data.takeaway: Broad system and service activity baseline.
data.what: Plaintext system and service messages (kernel, daemons, apps), typically rotated by logrotate.
data.why: Provides a broad timeline and context when specialized logs are sparse.
data.question: What system events occurred around the incident?

data.name: systemd Journal
data.takeaway: Centralized log source, even when text logs rotate.
data.what: Binary systemd journal with structured fields for services and kernel events, queryable via journalctl.
data.why: Centralized evidence even if text logs are disabled; supports filtering by unit or time.
data.question: What services or system events were recorded?

data.name: Cron Jobs
data.takeaway: Scheduled tasks used for automation or persistence.
data.what: Scheduled tasks defined in system/user crontabs and /etc/cron.* directories, sometimes via anacron.
data.why: Common automation and persistence mechanism; shows periodic execution of scripts or commands.
data.question: What tasks run on a schedule?

data.name: Package Manager Logs
data.takeaway: Records software installs/removals with timestamps.
data.what: Package manager logs recording installs, upgrades, and removals with package versions and timestamps.
data.why: Shows software changes and timing of tool installation or removal.
data.question: What software changes happened recently?
corroborate: Auth logs for sudo install activity

data.name: SSH Keys
data.takeaway: Persistent access via trusted keys and known hosts.
data.what: Authorized_keys and known_hosts files storing trusted public keys and remote host fingerprints.
data.why: Reveals persistent access paths and trusted hosts tied to lateral movement.
data.question: Which keys were trusted or used for access?

data.name: Login Records
data.takeaway: Durable login evidence even after text logs rotate.
data.what: Binary login databases tracking successful and failed sessions (wtmp, btmp, lastlog), used by last/lastb.
data.why: Durable login evidence even after text logs rotate; helps confirm session timelines.
data.question: When were logins successful or failed?

data.name: Audit Logs (auditd)
data.takeaway: Detailed syscall and file access logging when configured.
data.what: Linux Audit Framework logs capturing syscalls, file access, user commands, and security events based on configured rules.
data.why: Provides granular evidence of process execution, file access, and privilege use beyond standard logs.
data.question: What specific actions were taken at the syscall level?

data.name: Systemd Units
data.takeaway: Service definitions reveal persistence and startup behavior.
data.what: Systemd unit files (.service, .timer, .socket) defining services, timers, and socket activation for automatic execution.
data.why: Common persistence mechanism; malicious units may hide in user directories or override legitimate services.
data.question: What services or timers are configured to run automatically?

data.name: /proc Filesystem
data.takeaway: Live process and system state for running system analysis.
data.what: Virtual filesystem exposing kernel and process information including command lines, environment variables, file descriptors, and memory maps.
data.why: Essential for live response to identify running processes, open files, network connections, and deleted-but-open files.
data.question: What processes are running and what resources are they using?
location: Live system only; not available in disk images

data.name: Environment Files
data.takeaway: Shell startup files used for persistence and environment manipulation.
data.what: Per-user and system-wide shell configuration files (.bashrc, .bash_profile, .profile, /etc/profile.d/) executed on login or shell start.
data.why: Attackers inject malicious commands or PATH manipulation for persistence; changes may be subtle.
data.question: Were shell startup files modified for persistence?

data.name: User Accounts
data.takeaway: User and group definitions reveal account creation and privilege.
data.what: System files defining user accounts (passwd), password hashes (shadow), groups, and sudoers configuration.
data.why: Shows account creation, UID/GID assignments, and privilege escalation paths via sudo.
data.question: What accounts exist and what privileges do they have?

data.name: Web Server Logs
data.takeaway: HTTP request logs for web shell and exploitation analysis.
data.what: Access and error logs from Apache, Nginx, or other web servers recording requests, response codes, user agents, and errors.
data.why: Critical for identifying web shell access, exploitation attempts, and initial access vectors.
data.question: What web requests indicate malicious activity?
corroborate: File system for web shells in document root
Auth logs for related user activity

data.name: /tmp and /dev/shm
data.takeaway: World-writable locations often used for staging and execution.
data.what: Temporary filesystems (/tmp disk-backed, /dev/shm memory-backed) writable by all users, commonly used for staging tools or payloads.
data.why: Attackers frequently stage tools, scripts, or payloads here; memory-backed /dev/shm avoids disk writes.
data.question: Are there suspicious files or recently executed tools in temp directories?
corroborate: Process listing for executables in temp paths

data.name: /etc/hosts
data.takeaway: Static DNS overrides for redirection or blocking.
data.what: Static hostname-to-IP mappings that override DNS resolution, used legitimately for local aliases or maliciously for redirection.
data.why: Attackers may redirect security update servers or C2 domains; defenders may block known-bad domains.
data.question: Has DNS resolution been manipulated via /etc/hosts?

data.name: Kernel Logs
data.takeaway: Hardware, driver, and kernel-level events including security messages.
data.what: Kernel ring buffer (dmesg) and persistent logs (kern.log) containing hardware events, driver messages, and kernel security events.
data.why: Can reveal hardware attacks, driver exploits, kernel module loading, and security subsystem events.
data.question: What kernel-level events occurred, including module loads or security alerts?
corroborate: Auth logs for related user activity

data.name: Core Dumps
data.takeaway: Crash dumps can reveal exploitation or malware behavior.
data.what: Process memory dumps generated on crashes, containing program state, memory contents, and crash context.
data.why: Exploitation attempts cause crashes; core dumps capture process state at time of failure.
data.question: Did any processes crash, and what was their state?

data.name: SUID/SGID Binaries
data.takeaway: Privilege escalation vectors via setuid/setgid executables.
data.what: Executables with SUID or SGID bits set, running with elevated privileges regardless of the calling user.
data.why: Attackers add SUID bits to backdoors or exploit vulnerable SUID binaries for privilege escalation.
data.question: Are there unexpected SUID/SGID binaries or recent changes?
corroborate: Package manager to verify legitimate SUID files

data.name: at Jobs
data.takeaway: One-time scheduled tasks, alternative to cron.
data.what: Jobs scheduled via the at command for one-time execution at a specified time.
data.why: Less commonly monitored than cron; attackers may use for delayed execution or persistence.
data.question: Are there scheduled one-time jobs that shouldn't exist?
corroborate: Cron jobs for other scheduled tasks
location: atq command to list pending jobs

data.name: Linux Capabilities
data.takeaway: Fine-grained privileges that can enable escalation without full root.
data.what: POSIX capabilities assigned to executables or processes, granting specific privileges without full root access.
data.why: Misconfigured capabilities (e.g., CAP_SETUID) can enable privilege escalation.
data.question: Do any binaries have dangerous capabilities assigned?
corroborate: SUID/SGID binaries for other escalation paths

data.name: LD_PRELOAD / Library Injection
data.takeaway: Shared library hijacking for persistence or credential theft.
data.what: Environment variables and configuration files that force loading of malicious shared libraries before legitimate ones.
data.why: Attackers inject malicious libraries to intercept function calls, steal credentials, or maintain persistence.
data.question: Are there unauthorized preload configurations or suspicious libraries?

data.name: FSEvents
data.takeaway: File system change journal with historical activity.
data.what: macOS file system event store recording file and folder changes, used by Spotlight and Time Machine.
data.why: Provides historical record of file system activity even after files are deleted.
data.question: What file system changes occurred on this system?

data.name: Spotlight Metadata
data.takeaway: Indexed file content and metadata, including deleted files.
data.what: macOS search index containing file metadata, content snippets, and attributes for indexed files.
data.why: May contain evidence of files that no longer exist; useful for keyword searches.
data.question: What files existed or contained specific content?

data.name: Quarantine Events
data.takeaway: Records downloaded files with source URLs and timestamps.
data.what: Database tracking files downloaded from the internet, including source URLs, download timestamps, and application used.
data.why: Proves files were downloaded from specific URLs; similar to Windows Zone.Identifier.
data.question: What files were downloaded, from where, and when?

data.name: Unified Logs
data.takeaway: Centralized logging for all system and application events with rich filtering capabilities.
data.what: macOS unified logging system (introduced in 10.12) consolidating kernel, system, and application logs into a compressed binary format with structured fields, subsystems, categories, and multiple log levels. Supports predicate-based filtering for precise queries.
data.why: Primary and often only source for system activity on modern macOS. Contains authentication events, process execution, network activity, and application behavior. Traditional log files are largely deprecated.
data.question: What system and application events occurred?
location: /var/db/uuidtext/ - UUID to string mappings for log messages
Live logs in memory (not persisted unless collected)

data.name: Launch Agents / Daemons
data.takeaway: Primary persistence mechanism on macOS.
data.what: Property list files defining programs that run at login (agents) or boot (daemons), with triggers and configurations.
data.why: Most common macOS persistence mechanism; malicious plists may hide in user directories.
data.question: What programs are configured to run automatically?

data.name: TCC Database
data.takeaway: Privacy permission grants for applications.
data.what: Transparency, Consent, and Control database tracking which applications have been granted privacy permissions (camera, microphone, full disk access, etc.).
data.why: Shows which apps have sensitive permissions; attackers may grant permissions to malicious tools.
data.question: Which applications have been granted sensitive permissions?

data.name: Keychain
data.takeaway: Stored credentials and certificates.
data.what: macOS credential storage containing passwords, certificates, keys, and secure notes, protected by user password.
data.why: Attackers with user access may dump keychain contents; shows what credentials were stored.
data.question: What credentials were stored on this system?

data.name: Known Networks
data.takeaway: WiFi connection history with timestamps.
data.what: Database of WiFi networks the system has connected to, including SSIDs, security types, and connection timestamps.
data.why: Shows location history based on network connections; useful for timeline analysis.
data.question: What WiFi networks has this system connected to?

data.name: Login Items
data.takeaway: Applications launched at user login.
data.what: User-configured applications that launch automatically when the user logs in, separate from Launch Agents.
data.why: Simple persistence mechanism; check for unexpected applications.
data.question: What applications start at user login?
location: System Preferences > Users & Groups > Login Items

data.name: Sysmon Logs
data.takeaway: Enhanced process, network, and file monitoring when deployed.
data.what: Microsoft Sysinternals tool that logs detailed process creation, network connections, file creation, registry changes, and process access events to the Windows Event Log.
data.why: Provides visibility into LSASS access (Event ID 10), process injection, and command-line arguments not captured by default Windows logging.
data.question: What detailed process and network activity occurred on this system?
location: Requires Sysmon to be installed and configured

data.name: Outlook Artifacts
data.takeaway: Email storage and attachment cache for phishing investigations.
data.what: Microsoft Outlook data files (OST/PST), attachment cache, and temporary files storing emails, attachments, and metadata.
data.why: Critical for tracing phishing attacks; attachment cache may contain malicious payloads even after email deletion.
data.question: What emails were received and what attachments were opened?

data.name: Print Spooler
data.takeaway: Print job history for hardcopy exfiltration detection.
data.what: Windows Print Spooler service logs and spool files (.SPL, .SHD) recording print job metadata including document names, timestamps, and printer destinations.
data.why: Useful for insider threat investigations where documents may have been printed for physical exfiltration.
data.question: What documents were printed, and when?
corroborate: Event Logs for print events (Event ID 307)
location: Spool files may be deleted after job completion

data.name: Windows Activity Timeline
data.takeaway: Rich user activity history including app usage, file access, and cross-device sync.
data.what: SQLite database tracking user activities including application usage, file opens, clipboard history, and browser activity. Introduced in Windows 10 1803 as part of Timeline feature. Can sync across devices via Microsoft account.
data.why: Provides detailed user activity timeline with timestamps, even for activities that don't leave traditional artifacts. Shows what users were doing and when, including activities synced from other devices.
data.question: What applications did the user interact with and what files did they access?
corroborate: Jump Lists for app-specific file access

Key Tables.tables: Core activity records with timestamps and payload

keyFields: AppId - JSON blob with application identifiers (exe path, AUMID)
ActivityType - 5=Open app, 6=Open file/URI, 10=Clipboard, 16=Copy/Paste
Payload - Base64/JSON with activity details (file paths, URLs)
StartTime/EndTime - Activity duration timestamps
PlatformDeviceId - Identifies source device for synced activities
ClipboardPayload - Clipboard content for Type 10 activities

data.name: Office Document Metadata
data.takeaway: Document metadata reveals authorship, edit history, and potential macro threats.
data.what: Microsoft Office documents (DOCX, XLSX, PPTX, legacy DOC/XLS/PPT) contain rich metadata including author names, creation/modification times, revision counts, company names, and embedded objects. Legacy OLE formats may contain macro code.
data.why: Metadata can reveal true document origin, authorship, and edit history even when file timestamps are modified. Macros and embedded objects are common malware delivery vectors. Useful for attribution and phishing investigations.
data.question: Who created this document, when was it actually authored, and does it contain malicious content?
corroborate: Prefetch for application execution after opening
location: ~$<filename> - Temporary owner files while document is open
keyFields: Core Properties: dc:creator, dc:title, dcterms:created, dcterms:modified
Extended Properties: Application, AppVersion, Company, TotalTime (edit minutes)
Custom Properties: User-defined metadata fields
Revision Number: Indicates how many times document was saved
Last Modified By: Last person to save the document
Template: Source template may indicate origin

data.name: Cloud Storage Clients
data.takeaway: Local sync databases reveal cloud file access and sync history.
data.what: Desktop sync clients for OneDrive, Dropbox, Google Drive, and similar services maintain local SQLite databases tracking synced files, sync status, deleted items, and sharing metadata. These persist even when files are removed from the cloud.
data.why: Reveals files that existed in cloud storage, sharing activity, and data exfiltration via cloud sync. Local databases may contain evidence of files deleted from the cloud. Critical for insider threat and data theft investigations.
data.question: What files were synced to/from cloud storage, and what was shared externally?
corroborate: File system for synced file content
Browser history for web interface access
keyFields: File paths and names (even for deleted cloud files)
Sharing status and shared link recipients
Sync timestamps (local vs cloud)
File size and hash values
Account email addresses

data.name: Windows Push Notifications
data.takeaway: Toast notification history reveals app activity and message content.
data.what: SQLite database storing Windows push notification history including toast notifications, badges, and tiles. Contains notification content, timestamps, and source applications. Introduced in Windows 10.
data.why: Notifications may contain message previews from chat apps, email subjects, calendar reminders, and other sensitive content. Shows application activity even when the app itself leaves minimal artifacts.
data.question: What notifications did the user receive, and from which applications?

Key Tables.tables: App icons and images for notifications

keyFields: Payload - XML content of the notification (may include message text)
Type - Notification type (toast, badge, tile)
HandlerId - Links to source application
ArrivalTime - When notification was received
ExpiryTime - When notification expires
PayloadType - toast, badge, tileLarge, etc.

data.name: IconCache Database
data.takeaway: Cached program icons prove applications existed even after deletion.
data.what: Windows maintains a cache of application icons in thumbcache-style database files. Contains icon images extracted from executables, providing evidence of programs that existed on the system.
data.why: Icon cache entries persist after programs are uninstalled or deleted. Can prove a specific application was present on the system even when all other traces have been removed.
data.question: What applications existed on this system, including deleted ones?
keyFields: Icon images at various resolutions (16x16 through 1024x1024)
Indexed by executable path hash
May contain icons for deleted programs
Use thumbcache_viewer or similar tools to extract
Compare extracted icons to known malware icons

data.name: KnowledgeC.db
data.takeaway: Comprehensive user activity database tracking app usage, device interactions, and screen time.
data.what: SQLite database maintained by the Knowledge framework (knowledged daemon) that tracks extensive user activity including application usage, Safari browsing, media playback, device sleep/wake cycles, bluetooth connections, and screen time. One of the richest forensic artifacts on macOS.
data.why: Provides detailed timeline of user activity with precise timestamps. Shows what apps were in focus, how long they were used, and user interaction patterns. Critical for establishing user presence and activity during an incident.
data.question: What was the user doing on this system and when?
keyFields: ZSTREAMNAME - Activity type: /app/usage, /safari/history, /device/isLocked, /audio/outputRoute
ZVALUESTRING - Application bundle ID or activity identifier
ZSTARTDATE/ZENDDATE - Activity duration (Mac absolute: seconds since 2001-01-01)
ZSECONDSFROMGMT - Timezone offset for the activity
ZSTRUCTUREDMETADATA.Z_DKAPPLICATIONACTIVITYMETADATAKEY__ACTIVITYTYPE - Detailed app activity
Use mac_apt or KAPE for parsing

data.name: Hiberfil.sys / Pagefile.sys
data.takeaway: Disk-based memory artifacts that can reveal passwords, encryption keys, and process data.
data.what: Hiberfil.sys contains a compressed copy of RAM written during hibernation. Pagefile.sys (and swapfile.sys on Win10+) contain memory pages swapped to disk during normal operation. Both can contain sensitive data from memory including passwords, encryption keys, and process memory.
data.why: Enables partial memory forensics without live acquisition. May contain decryption keys for BitLocker/VeraCrypt, plaintext passwords, chat messages, and evidence of running processes. Persists across reboots.
data.question: What sensitive data or process memory can be recovered from disk?
keyFields: Hiberfil.sys: Compressed RAM image, decompress with Volatility or hibernation-recon
Pagefile.sys: Unstructured, use strings/bulk_extractor for keyword searching
Look for: passwords, URLs, chat fragments, encryption keys, process memory
Compression: XPRESS (Win8+) or LZ (older)
Size: Typically 40-100% of RAM for hiberfil, configurable for pagefile

data.name: $LogFile (NTFS Transaction Log)
data.takeaway: NTFS transaction log that can recover very recent file operations even when MFT is overwritten.
data.what: NTFS journaling log that records all metadata changes to the file system before they're committed. Contains a circular buffer of recent operations including file creation, deletion, rename, and attribute changes. Separate from and more granular than $UsnJrnl.
data.why: Can recover evidence of very recent file operations (typically last few hours) with high precision. May reveal file operations that occurred between $MFT updates or when $UsnJrnl has rolled over.
data.question: What file operations occurred in the last few hours that might not appear elsewhere?
keyFields: Redo/Undo operations for each transaction
File reference numbers linking to $MFT entries
Operation types: CreateFile, DeleteFile, SetAttributes, RenameFile
LSN (Log Sequence Number) for ordering operations
Parse with LogFileParser, NTFS Log Tracker, or Autopsy

data.name: WSL Artifacts
data.takeaway: Linux filesystem and artifacts running inside Windows - increasingly used for tools and evasion.
data.what: Windows Subsystem for Linux creates a Linux environment with its own filesystem, bash history, logs, and artifacts. WSL1 stores files in a Windows-accessible location; WSL2 uses a virtual disk (ext4.vhdx). Attackers may use WSL to run Linux tools or evade Windows-focused detection.
data.why: Malware and attackers increasingly leverage WSL to execute Linux tools on Windows, access Linux-native exploits, or hide activity from Windows security tools. Full Linux artifact analysis applies within the WSL environment.
data.question: Was WSL used on this system, and what Linux activity occurred within it?
corroborate: Windows Event Logs for WSL service
Standard Linux artifacts within WSL filesystem
keyFields: rootfs/home/<user>/.bash_history - Command history
rootfs/var/log/ - Linux system logs
rootfs/etc/passwd, /etc/shadow - User accounts
rootfs/tmp/ - Temporary files and staged tools
ext4.vhdx can be mounted on Linux for analysis
Check for wsl.exe in Prefetch as indicator of use

data.name: iOS/iTunes Backups
data.takeaway: Mobile device evidence preserved on desktop - messages, photos, app data, and more.
data.what: iTunes and Finder create backups of iOS devices containing databases, preferences, and files from the mobile device. Includes messages (SMS/iMessage), call history, contacts, photos, Safari history, and third-party app data. May be encrypted with user-chosen password.
data.why: Mobile devices often contain critical evidence but may be locked or unavailable. Desktop backups provide access to substantial mobile data including messages and app data. Unencrypted backups are immediately accessible; encrypted backups require the backup password.
data.question: What mobile device data is preserved in desktop backups?
corroborate: Desktop browser history for iCloud web access
File system timestamps for backup timing
location: Each device has a UDID-named folder containing backup files

Key Files.tables: File inventory with domains and paths
Device info, backup date, iOS version

Key Databases (hashed filenames).tables: Call log with numbers and duration

keyFields: Manifest.db maps hashed filenames to original paths
Domain field indicates source app (HomeDomain, AppDomain, etc.)
Encrypted backups require password - check Keychain for stored password
Use iphone-backup-analyzer, iExplorer, or commercial mobile forensic tools
Third-party app data in AppDomain-* files

data.name: WBEM Repository
data.takeaway: Raw WMI database files for offline analysis of WMI persistence and configuration.
data.what: The WBEM (Web-Based Enterprise Management) repository stores all WMI classes, instances, and subscriptions in a proprietary database format. Contains the same data queryable via live WMI but accessible for offline forensic analysis.
data.why: WMI persistence (event subscriptions) is a common attack technique. The repository allows analysis of WMI artifacts from disk images without live system access. Can reveal persistence mechanisms, custom classes, and historical WMI activity.
data.question: What WMI persistence mechanisms or custom configurations exist on this system?
keyFields: __EventFilter - Trigger conditions for subscriptions
__EventConsumer - Actions executed (CommandLineEventConsumer, ActiveScriptEventConsumer)
__FilterToConsumerBinding - Links filters to consumers (persistence indicator)
Parse with PyWMIPersistenceFinder, WMI-Forensics, or Velociraptor
Look for non-standard namespaces beyond root\subscription

data.name: Dock & Finder Preferences
data.takeaway: Application usage patterns and folder access from Dock and Finder settings.
data.what: macOS stores Dock configuration (pinned apps, recent apps) and Finder preferences (sidebar items, recent folders, window positions) in plist files. These reveal commonly used applications and folder navigation patterns.
data.why: Shows user's frequently accessed applications and folders. Dock persistent apps indicate intentional placement; recent items show actual usage. Finder sidebar and recent folders reveal navigation patterns.
data.question: What applications and folders did the user frequently access?

recent-apps - Recently used applications (if enabled)
persistent-others - Folders/files pinned to Dock
FXRecentFolders - Recently accessed folders in Finder
FXDesktopVolumePositions - Mounted volume positions
FK* keys in finder.plist - Various Finder state data

File path, size, last modified time
Drive letter to UNC path mappings
Paths to deleted or external folders
